items.answer: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

items.prompt: What is non-immersive virtual reality system?
items.answer: From a systems point of view, virtual reality (VR) systems are broadly categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems because market applications offer varying degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive.

questions.question: What is cybersickness?
options: A headset hardware component used in augmented reality
A software development stage for building XR systems
A navigation optimization technique for VR content
A condition that can occur when people interact with virtual reality
questions.explanation: Cybersickness is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with VR technology.

questions.question: Which pair of symptoms are both mentioned as possible indicators of cybersickness?
options: Fatigue and hearing loss
Nausea and dryness of mouth
Dizziness and blurred vision
Nausea and chest pain
questions.explanation: Nausea, dryness of mouth, dizziness, and fatigue are listed as possible symptoms of cybersickness, while chest pain, blurred vision, and hearing loss are not.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the causes of cybersickness?
options: It is always caused by VR content
It is caused by multiple factors, not a single factor
It is caused by only one factor
It is always caused by headset hardware
questions.explanation: Cybersickness can be caused by many factors rather than by a single factor.

questions.question: Why is reducing cybersickness important for VR systems?
options: It improves usability and makes VR more appealing to a wider range of users
It removes the need for VR tracking
It increases the frame rate of VR content
It lowers the price of VR headsets
questions.explanation: Reducing cybersickness greatly enhances overall user experience, which improves the usability and acceptability of VR systems and makes them more appealing to more people.

data.text: Cybersickness (CS), also known as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality. It can be caused by many factors and is indicated by symptoms such as nausea, headache, and dizziness. Reducing the impact of cybersickness is very important for the usability and acceptability of VR systems.
points: Cybersickness (CS) is a condition that affects individuals interacting with virtual reality.
Symptoms such as nausea, headache, and dizziness indicate the onset of cybersickness.
Cybersickness can be caused by many different factors.
Reducing the impact of cybersickness is important for the usability and appeal of VR systems.

questions.question: In a causes framework for cybersickness, what are the two broad categories of causes?
options: Causes and mitigation
Evaluation and mitigation
Hardware and VR content
Internal and external factors
questions.explanation: Cybersickness causes are broadly internal factors and external factors, with external factors comprising hardware and VR content.

questions.question: Which of the following is an internal user-related factor that can increase the likelihood of cybersickness?
options: VR content
Display resolution
Headset latency
Motion sickness susceptibility
questions.explanation: Internal factors are individual characteristics or conditions such as motion sickness susceptibility, physical condition, and emotional condition; hardware factors and VR content are external.

questions.question: How are motion sickness susceptibility and cybersickness generally related?
options: Motion sickness susceptibility is unrelated to cybersickness risk
Higher motion sickness susceptibility is associated with higher cybersickness risk
Motion sickness susceptibility only matters when VR content is controllable
Lower motion sickness susceptibility is associated with higher cybersickness risk
questions.explanation: There is a positive correlation between motion sickness susceptibility and cybersickness risk, so higher motion sickness susceptibility is likely to lead to more severe cybersickness symptoms.

questions.question: Why might female users of head-mounted displays be associated with increased cybersickness?
options: Inter-pupillary distance fit may be harder to find, affecting stereoscopic vision
They usually have greater retinal eccentricity
They are more likely to use a standing posture
They usually have higher headset latency
questions.explanation: A possible reason is inter-pupillary distance fit because inter-pupillary distance determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit.

questions.question: How does physical position affect cybersickness susceptibility when using the same VR system?
options: A sitting posture is likely to induce more cybersickness than standing
Physical position has no effect on cybersickness
A standing posture is likely to induce more or more severe cybersickness than sitting
A standing posture matters only for users with neurological conditions
questions.explanation: Using a VR system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cybersickness, or more severe cybersickness, than using the same system while sitting.

data.text: Cybersickness is caused by both internal factors, such as age, gender, and motion sickness susceptibility, and external factors like hardware and VR content. Specific physical conditions, including poor sleep quality, greater retinal eccentricity, and neurological conditions can increase susceptibility. Additionally, physical posture and negative emotional conditions can heighten the risk, though repeated exposure may reduce the severity of symptoms.
points: Cybersickness is caused by internal and external factors, with external factors including hardware and VR content.
Internal factors include individual characteristics like age, gender, motion sickness susceptibility, physical condition, and emotional condition.
Age-related sensitivity varies and is more notable in controllable content, while gender differences remain inconclusive.
High motion sickness susceptibility, poor sleep quality, greater retinal eccentricity, and neurological conditions increase the risk of cybersickness.
Using a system in a standing posture or experiencing negative emotions can also increase the likelihood of cybersickness.

questions.question: How does increasing VR display resolution from 1K to 4K affect cybersickness?
options: It is substantially reduced from 1K to 2K, with little further reduction at 3K or 4K.
It increases substantially from 1K to 2K, then remains stable.
It is reduced only when moving from 3K to 4K.
It is substantially reduced at each step from 1K to 4K.
questions.explanation: A resolution study found a substantial reduction in cybersickness from 1K to 2K, but no significant further reduction from 2K to 3K or 3K to 4K.

questions.question: In HMD-based VR, what is the effect of higher latency?
options: It affects only users with low motion-sickness susceptibility.
It decreases the likelihood of cybersickness.
It increases the likelihood of cybersickness.
It has no effect unless latency jitter is high.
questions.explanation: Latency is the time gap between a physical movement and its virtual-world change, and in HMD-based VR, more latency makes cybersickness more likely.

questions.question: What is latency jitter in VR?
options: Variability in the time gap between a physical movement and its virtual reflection.
A user’s susceptibility to motion sickness.
A fixed time gap between a physical movement and its virtual reflection.
The difference in cybersickness between HMD and monitor users.
questions.explanation: Latency jitter is variability in latency, which can create irregular timing and lead to discomfort, disorientation, and cybersickness.

questions.question: Which display comparison is associated with more cybersickness?
options: Using a panoramic screen instead of a VR headset.
Using a flat-screen display instead of a VR headset.
Using a VR headset instead of a flat-screen display.
Using a non-immersive display instead of an HMD-based display.
questions.explanation: HMD-based or VR headset displays are associated with more cybersickness than conventional monitors or non-immersive systems, and a study found VR headset users experienced more cybersickness than flat-screen users.

questions.question: Which VR input comparison is associated with less cybersickness?
options: Using steering with handlebars instead of a joystick.
Using a gamepad instead of a hand controller.
Using a gamepad and a hand controller equally.
Using a hand controller instead of a gamepad.
questions.explanation: Input method can influence cybersickness, and a gamepad causes less cybersickness than a hand controller, while motion controls such as handlebars may cause more than non-motion controls such as a joystick.

data.text: Hardware is a category of external factors that can induce cybersickness in virtual reality. Display resolution reduces cybersickness up to 2K, but shows no significant reduction from 2K to 3K or 4K. Additionally, latency and its variability increase the likelihood and severity of cybersickness, while the display type, its quality, and the input method used also influence these levels.
points: Hardware is a category of external factors that can induce cybersickness in virtual reality.
Display resolution reduces cybersickness up to 2K, but shows no significant reduction from 2K to 3K or 4K.
Latency and its variability, known as jitter, increase the likelihood and severity of cybersickness.
The display type, its quality, and the input method used can influence cybersickness levels.

questions.question: Which of the following is an internal factor in the causes of cybersickness?
options: VR content
The user's age
Display type
Latency
questions.explanation: Age is listed as an internal factor, while VR content, display type, and latency are external factors.

questions.question: Which of the following is a hardware factor among the causes of cybersickness?
options: The user's age
VR content
Latency jitter
The user's gender
questions.explanation: Hardware factors include display type, latency, latency jitter, resolution, and input technology; gender, age, and VR content are not hardware factors.

questions.question: The causes of cybersickness are broadly divided into which two categories?
options: Age factors and gender factors
Hardware factors and content factors
Display factors and input factors
Internal factors and external factors
questions.explanation: The causes are broadly divided into internal factors and external factors. Hardware and content factors are subdivisions of external factors, not the broad division.

data.text: Cybersickness is caused by internal factors like age and gender, as well as external factors like hardware and content. Virtual reality content is specifically identified as one of these external factors.
points: Cybersickness is caused by internal factors like age and gender, and external factors like hardware and content.
Virtual reality content is an external factor that contributes to cybersickness.

questions.question: Why does reducing cybersickness matter for a virtual reality system that is defined as an interactive computer-generated sensory environment?
questions.reference_answer: A virtual reality system is a system with an artificial environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens. Reducing cybersickness is important for such systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and supports usability and acceptability. It also makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

questions.question: How does prior or repeated exposure to virtual reality relate to the link between motion sickness susceptibility and cybersickness?
questions.reference_answer: Motion sickness occurs when the brain receives conflicting signals from various sensory organs, and virtual reality recreates realistic movement and visual environments, so motion sickness susceptibility tends to co-occur with cyber sickness susceptibility. Studies indicate a positive correlation between motion sickness susceptibility and cyber sickness risk, with higher susceptibility likely producing more severe cyber sickness symptoms. Prior or repeated exposure to virtual reality can reduce that effect and reduce cybersickness severity over time.

questions.question: How do latency and display resolution differ as hardware factors that can cause cybersickness?
questions.reference_answer: Latency is the time delay between a user's movement and the corresponding change in the virtual world, and in head-mounted display-based virtual reality cybersickness increases as latency increases. Latency jitter is variability in that latency and can create irregularities, inconsistencies, discomfort, disorientation, and cybersickness. Display resolution reduces cybersickness only up to a point: a study found substantial reduction from 1K to 2K, but no significant further reduction from 2K to 3K or from 3K to 4K.

questions.question: How can inter-pupillary distance fit explain why female head-mounted display users may experience more cybersickness?
questions.reference_answer: Stereoscopic vision makes users perceive two-dimensional images as three-dimensional objects and space, and inter-pupillary distance determines stereoscopic vision. Female head-mounted display use is associated with increased cybersickness, possibly because a greater proportion of female users have trouble finding a good inter-pupillary distance fit. This suggests that virtual reality displays should have a wider inter-pupillary distance adjustable range for female users.
